lectures.title: Basic Structure Doctrine and the Landmark Cases

parts.t: What the Basic Structure doctrine is
items: **Basic Structure Doctrine:** core structural features of the Constitution that cannot be abrogated or destroyed even via Article 368.
**First propounded in:** Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973).
**Foundational legal principle:** Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution is plenary but limited; it cannot abrogate, alter, or destroy its essential foundation / basic features.
The term "Basic Structure" is **not** defined in Part XX of the Constitution: it is a judicially formulated concept.

parts.t: Amendment battle: Article 368 vs Part III
items: **Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951):** upheld Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights under Art. 368; upheld the 1st CAA.
**Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965):** reaffirmed that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights; upheld the 17th CAA.
**Shankari Prasad & Sajjan Singh:** ruled that ordinary law under Art. 13(2) does not include constitutional amendments under Art. 368 (Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights).

**Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967):** reversed / overruled the earlier rulings; held that an amendment is "law" under Art. 13(2) and Parliament CANNOT amend Fundamental Rights (cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right).
**Golaknath:** the first time Parliament's amending power was limited.
**Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973):** Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution (including FRs), but cannot alter, damage or destroy the "Basic Structure".
**Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980):** reinforced / reaffirmed the Basic Structure doctrine.
**Bench:** delivered by the largest bench, 13 Judges; 7:6 majority.
**Ruling:** the 13-Judge Bench propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine; Parliament can amend FRs but cannot alter / destroy the Basic Structure.
**Preamble:** recognized the Preamble as part of the Constitution.
**Golaknath vs Kesavananda:** Golaknath completely prohibited amending FRs; Kesavananda allowed amending FRs subject to the Basic Structure boundary.
**Limited amending power:** reaffirmed that a limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature.
**Clauses struck down:** invalidated clauses (4) and (5) of Art. 368 inserted by the 42nd CAA.
**FRs and DPSPs:** struck down clauses giving absolute precedence to DPSPs over FRs; restored the balance between Part III and Part IV.
**Kesavananda vs Minerva Mills:** Kesavananda propounded the Basic Structure doctrine; Minerva Mills reinforced / approved it and struck down unconditional DPSP precedence.

parts.t: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) and S.R. Bommai (1994)
items: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
**Ruling:** struck down parts of the 39th Amendment that barred judicial review of election disputes of the PM and Speaker.
**Key issue:** judicial scrutiny of high constitutional elections; free & fair elections are in the Basic Structure.
**Linked amendment:** 39th CAA (Art. 329A); nullified by the 44th Amendment.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
**Article 356:** laid guidelines against arbitrary misuse of Article 356 (President's Rule); made the proclamation subject to judicial review.
**Basic features:** held secularism and federalism as basic features; reaffirmed the Preamble as an integral part.
**Communalism & secularism:** ruled that Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution; state governments acting against secularism can be dismissed under Article 356.

parts.t: Judicial review and independence of the judiciary
items: **Judicial Review as Basic Structure:** in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980) and L. Chandra Kumar (1997), Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was explicitly declared an inviolable, integral part of the Basic Structure.
**Article 368:** Parliament cannot abrogate Judicial Review even via Article 368.
**Review of Constitutional Amendments:** constitutional amendments are themselves subject to Judicial Review on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine.
**NJAC:** struck down in 2015 because executive involvement infringed upon the Independence of the Judiciary, which is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

parts.t: Cases at a glance and chronology
items: Propounded Basic Structure Doctrine; Preamble is part
Judicial scrutiny of high constitutional elections
Reinforced Basic Structure; balance between FR & DPSP
Judicial Review of President's Rule; Preamble integral
**Chronology:** A.K. Gopalan (1950) -- Shankari Prasad (1951) -- Champakam Dorairajan (1951) -- Berubari (1960) -- Sajjan Singh (1965) -- Golaknath (1967) -- Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
**Chronology (continued):** Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) -- Maneka Gandhi (1978) -- Minerva Mills (1980) -- Kihoto Hollohan (1993) -- S.R. Bommai (1994).
**Textual Fallacy:** "The term 'Basic Structure' is explicitly defined in Part XX of the Constitution" - FALSE (judicially formulated concept).
**Fundamental Rights Absolute Immunity Trap:** "Fundamental Rights can never be amended post-Kesavananda" - FALSE.
**Correct Principle:** FRs can be amended, provided the amendment does not violate the Basic Structure.
